item.title: In-orbit operation of a programmable quantum photonic processor
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Demonstrated an in-orbit programmable quantum photonic processor operating on a nanosatellite, generating and manipulating two-photon states in a six-mode universal integrated circuit and observing two-photon Hong-Ou-Mandel interference.

Grade 0.526 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Simon Steiner, Peter Schiansky, Antonius Scherer, Riccardo Albiero, Mathias Dragosits, Zhenghao Yin, Martin Mauser, Patrik Zahálka, Raphael Pimenta, Cristóbal Melo, Cédric Léonard, Abhiram Rajan, Niki Di Giano, Antonino Caime, Roberto Osellame, Francesco Ceccarelli, Daniel Martínez, Tobias Guggemos, Iris Agresti, Philip Walther

Figure

Normalized two-photon coincidence counts plotted against the ppKTP crystal temperature, showing the characteristic Hong-Ou-Mandel interference dip observed during orbital operation across multiple days.

Asks

Can quantum interference conditions (spectral degeneracy, phase stability, and optical alignment) be established and maintained on a programmable photonic circuit in space?

But

Payload constrained to 10 W average power, 9.8 kg mass, and 15 x 15 x 45.3 cm volume; low-noise coincidence measurements restricted to ~30 min per 92 min orbit during Earth shadow due to sunlight leakage and radiation-induced detector noise.

Tools

Type-II SPDC in ppKTP crystal · 6x6 reconfigurable universal photonic integrated circuit (uPIC) · Single-photon avalanche photodiodes (SPADs) · Custom FPGA System on a Module (SoM)

Abstract

Quantum technologies promise computational capabilities beyond the reach of classical systems. A forward-looking application lies in satellite missions, which increasingly depend on onboard computing under stringent constraints on size, weight and power. Quantum photonics is particularly attractive here: photon interference can enhance the machine-learning models needed to process large onboard data volumes, at fixed hardware resources. However, harnessing this interference requires more than generating single photons, as they must remain mutually indistinguishable: a fragile condition that is hard to maintain within the technically demanding framework of a space mission, which includes a rocket launch, strong thermal drifts, and radiation. This is why quantum states of light, though already generated and transmitted in orbit for secure communication and fundamental tests, have never been used as a computational resource. Here, we report a programmable quantum photonic platform operating on a nanosatellite, processing two photons in a six-mode universal integrated circuit. By programming distinct unitaries and tuning the photons into indistinguishability, we observe two-photon interference, establishing the on-board generation, manipulation and detection of non-classical light. This extends space-based technologies towards in-orbit quantum-assisted computing, for instance local encoding of Earth-observation data, or nodes in a distributed quantum network.

item.title: Strong coupling of a reconfigurable ¹⁷¹Yb atom array to a tunable telecom-band nanofiber cavity
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Strong atom-cavity coupling on the telecom 3P0↔3D1 transition of 171Yb at 1389 nm reaches single-atom internal cooperativity Cin=5.6(1.0) with single-atom coupling strength g/2π=1.86(17) MHz. Collective coupling scales as N up to N=5 atoms across a ∼200 μm length.

Grade 0.470 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Hideki Ozawa, Neville Chen, Yusuke Hisai, Shunichiro Hashimoto, Kenichi N. Komagata, Remi T. Oddon, Shanjou Yang, Seitaro Horikawa, Seigo Kikura, Shigehito Miki, Takao Aoki, Tadayuki Yoshitake, Hideki Konishi, Shinichi Sunami, Akihisa Goban, Ryotaro Inoue

Figure

Cavity reflection as a function of detuning from the cavity resonance, showing the empty cavity dip (gray) versus vacuum Rabi splitting (purple) induced by a single trapped 171Yb atom positioned 1 μm from the nanofiber axis.

Asks

Can neutral atoms in a reconfigurable tweezer array achieve the single-atom strong-coupling cavity-QED regime directly on a telecom-band transition using a nanofiber cavity?

Before

Strong coupling in nanofiber cavities was previously demonstrated only with single trapped alkali atoms at non-telecom wavelengths (e.g. Kato 2015, Goban 2012), while prior telecom atom-cavity interfaces lacked single-atom strong coupling.

But

Operated with single-sided cavity geometry at 1 μm standoff from the nanofiber axis; internal loss rate κin/2π=1.28(6) MHz; entanglement rate projection of 40 kHz neglects detector and transmission losses.

Tools

550-nm-diameter nanofiber cavity with fiber Bragg gratings · 759-nm optical tweezer array · ¹⁷¹Yb atoms on ³P₀↔³D₁ transition at 1389 nm · cavity reflection spectroscopy

Abstract

Nanophotonic cavities provide strong atom-photon coupling in a compact, directly fiber-coupled geometry, while a reconfigurable array of ¹⁷¹Yb atoms combines high-fidelity gates with a metastable qubit state coupled directly to a telecom-band transition, making the two a natural interface between neutral-atom quantum processors and telecom quantum networks. Here, we realize strong atom-cavity coupling on the ³P₀ ↔³D₁ transition of ¹⁷¹Yb, establishing, to our knowledge, the first neutral-atom cavity-QED system to reach the single-atom strong-coupling regime on a telecom-band atomic transition. Reflection spectroscopy of a single-sided cavity yields a single-atom internal cooperativity of C_in=5.6(1.0) and collective coupling following √N scaling up to N=5 atoms, with homogeneous coupling at antinodes over ∼200 μm along the nanofiber. Thermal tuning of a fiber Bragg grating provides in situ control of the cavity outcoupling rate over two orders of magnitude from the undercoupled to the overcoupled regime, relevant for various atom-cavity protocols. We confirm compatibility with reconfigurable atom arrays by demonstrating 99.95(6)% imaging fidelity and trap lifetimes comparable to free-space array, at 1 μm from the nanofiber axis. Moreover, the diameter-engineered antireflection design of the nanofiber enables tweezer-based atom transport across the nanofiber with no measurable loss or heating at 4.5 μm above the nanofiber, supporting a two-layer architecture for the nanofiber-integrated atom array. From the demonstrated atom-cavity coupling, atom capacity, and cavity mode profile, we project time-multiplexed remote atom-atom entanglement generation at 40 kHz, with prospects for further scaling through technical enhancements and channel multiplexing.

item.title: Error Suppression in Distributed Quantum Computing with Heterogeneous-Distance Lattice Surgery
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery with an enlarged ancilla (dA=2d+1) spanning the inter-QPU boundary achieves logical readout error rates nearly independent of link noise, cutting 5−11−5 physical qubit sites by 28.4% compared to uniform distance-9 (373 vs 521 qubits).

Grade 0.446 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Cavity-based quantum networks with single atoms and optical photons” · Daniel Dilley, Anastashia Jebraeilli, Rayat Roy, Shobhit Gupta, Alvin Gonzales, Zain Saleem

Figure

Control-X decoding failure probability per CNOT plotted against physical link error probability plink from 10−3 to 10−2. Heterogeneous 5−11−5 stays nearly flat and matches uniform distance-9 at high link noise while outperforming uniform distance-5 and -7.

Asks

How effectively can additional fault-tolerant error protection be concentrated at a noisy quantum processor interface while preserving the code distance of local data patches?

Before

Uniform distance-3 and distance-5 implementations, which exhibit steep increases in logical error rates as link noise grows; at plink=10−2, heterogeneous 3−7−3 reduces decoding failure by factors of ≈13 and ≈19 relative to uniform distance-3.

But

Evaluated under circuit-level stochastic depolarizing noise with fixed local noise plocal=10−4; excludes idle noise, link-generation latency/failures, leakage, and correlated link faults. Requires more total inter-QPU gate applications despite fewer physical sites.

Tools

Rotated surface codes · 8-DAM (eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated) architecture · Traveling stabilizer syndrome scheduling · Circuit-level Stim simulations

Abstract

Distributed quantum computing requires fault-tolerant operations across inter-QPU links that can be substantially noisier than local gates. Uniformly increasing code distance provides additional protection but also enlarges data patches used for local storage and computation. Here, we introduce distributed heterogeneous-distance lattice surgery using an eight-data-patch ancilla-mediated (8-DAM) architecture, which will be useful for near-term quantum devices with less qubit overhead. In this architecture, the central ancilla spanning the inter-QPU boundary is enlarged while the data patches retain distance d. The protocol uses traveling stabilizers to suppress hook errors during merge and split operations between these unequal-distance patches. Circuit-level simulations of rotated surface codes at fixed local depolarizing noise show that logical-readout error rates depend only weakly on link noise. The resulting advantage over conventional lattice surgery grows as link errors increase. Comparisons with uniform distance implementations demonstrate comparable logical error suppression with reduced physical-qubit overhead. We also demonstrate how 8-DAM layouts support two simultaneous distributed logical CNOT operations between four logical data qubits using a single enlarged ancilla. At higher link noise, this construction yields lower logical error rates and more stability than two independent distributed logical CNOTs. These results support selective ancilla enlargement as a resource-efficient approach to fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.

item.title: Tensor Network Simulation of Dynamic Circuits
item.description:
Worth a look new method — DMRG-based tensor network simulation natively evaluates dynamic circuits via single-path stochastic sampling and multi-path branch ensemble tracking on MPS and TTN structures, achieving scalable branch propagation with bounded peak memory on 27-qubit random circuits.

Grade 0.437 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Innocenzo Fulginiti, Alessandro Poggiali, Christian Mendl

Figure

Runtime (left) and peak memory usage (right) versus qubit count for dynamic GHZ state preparation comparing unpruned multi-path simulation against single-path sampling with 16, 64, and 256 runs.

Asks

How can tensor-network DMRG algorithms be extended to classically simulate dynamic quantum circuits with mid-circuit measurements and classical feedforward without exponential path overhead?

But

Evaluated up to 27 qubits and depth 8; fixed bond dimensions χ∈{8,16,32}; multi-path branch count capped at M=8.

Tools

DMRG quantum circuit simulation · Matrix Product States (MPS) · Tree Tensor Networks (TTN) · Single-path stochastic sampling · Multi-path branch pruning

Abstract

Dynamic circuits, which incorporate mid-circuit measurements and classically controlled operations, extend the expressive power of quantum programs and are central to applications such as quantum error correction, state preparation, and distributed quantum algorithms. However, their classical simulation is challenging due to the exponential growth of execution branches induced by mid-circuit measurements. In this work, we develop a tensor network approach for simulating dynamic circuits by extending a DMRG-based method for quantum circuit simulation to support dynamic circuit operations. To address the exponential proliferation of execution branches, we introduce and compare two strategies: a single-path stochastic approach that samples individual measurement outcomes, and a multi-path approach that maintains an ensemble of branches. We benchmark these methods on standard dynamic circuits, including the teleportation protocol and GHZ state preparation, as well as on random dynamic circuits. Our analysis explores the trade-offs between simulation accuracy and computational efficiency. These results provide a practical and scalable framework for the classical simulation of dynamic circuits.
